Your argument makes no sense.

There are two components of skill in a first person shooter:

1. Aim or what is called "technical skill"

2. The second type is called cognitive skill. This is what we call game sense.

Aim is a closed skill. It does not interact with other players. There's only one way to use this skill - to aim as effectively as you possibly can. 

But what exactly is aim? Aim is nothing but muscle memory. Your brain remembers what intensity to push your muscles to replicate a movement by X degrees in-game.

It does not take effort to aim as it is entirely muscle memory. You simply perform an action with absolutely 0 effort on your part. It's a brain-dead skill. It requires no greater effort to be a good aimer than to be a bad one. Rather, it requires greater skill to be a bad aimer than a good aimer because good aim is simply muscle memory. It's not something that someone "tries" to do...

What is cognitive skill or game sense?

Game sense is simply a form of intuition developed after observing patterns in gameplay across multiple instances of events. The human brain is incredibly skilled at pattern observation, so cognitive skill or game sense is too, a passive skill. You just observe things and you develop an intuition as to what works and what doesn't. 

It takes no greater effort to realize that a player who is climbing a ledge is likely to be unable to retaliate from an attack for a brief moment or that a player rushing a corner is likely to have a teammate behind them. 

People who are good at games aren't "trying hard". They've just played enough that they have natural and effortless ability to move their muscle a certain way to replicate results and to understand the underworkings as well as the "meta" of a game.

It takes no greater effort to be good at a game. No one is "trying hard".
